title: Adoption of modern digital innovations: a systematic review of social impacts in online community forums - Social Network Analysis and Mining
content:
## Abstract

Scholars have employed multiple methodologies to examine the correlation between different social networks and the extent of technological adoption among consumers. Although there has been a lack of uniformity in understanding and operationalising fundamental networking site constituents, the adoption and implementation of said analytical paradigms have yielded a wealth of revelations. To address these issues, this research examines the relationship between social networks and consumer adoption of digital technologies, addressing inconsistencies in defining and operationalising key components of social media platforms. Using the Community, Interference, Correlation, and Results (CICR) framework, the study evaluates existing paradigms and their limitations, including inconsistencies in cognitive models and research scenarios. Key recommendations include developing a systematic methodology for investigating the correlation between social media connectivity and technology adoption, considering socio-demographic variables as moderators and behavioral attributes as mediators. The study examines the CICR model’s limitations, including inconsistencies in cognitive paradigms, research scenarios, survey focus areas, and recent advancements. It proposes a systematic methodology to explore the correlation between social media connectivity and consumer technology adoption within the information communication technology (ICT) context, covering hardware, software, and devices such as smartphones, computers, and related applications. This research emphasizes the role of social media in shaping consumer attitudes toward digitalisation and highlights its implications for advancing ICT.

### Similar content being viewed by others

## 1 Introduction

According to a growing corpus of studies, modern technology adoption is a critical determinant of effective data systems (Ortega et al. 2022; Chew et al. 2022; Tsai 2017). As a result of this realisation, scholars have focused their efforts on identifying the elements that impact people’s acceptance of consumer technology (Abouzahra and Ghasemaghaei 2022). Researchers in both the field of communication management and the field of behavioural science have taken an interest in consumers’ use of advanced technologies since it is frequently regarded as an expression of behaviour. The authors of a study (Pirani et al. 2023) contend that an individual’s point of view on a certain conduct is an essential component in describing that behaviour. To paraphrase what was said by Hoffmann and Akbar (2023), authors believe that both internal and outside factors have an effect on the perceptions that clients have of a company. The assumption that consumers’ perceptions of innovation mirror their individual levels of use is supported by a growing amount of scholarly data (Mc Hugh et al. 2023; De Vos et al. 2022; Baierl et al. 2022).

The technological acceptability paradigm (TAP) (Oyman et al. 2022; Katebi et al. 2022), is the dominant frame of reference that is commonly used to forecast the use of client technologies. For the purpose of measuring consumer perception, TAP employs two fundamental indicators, namely perceived usability (PU) and perceived ease of usage (PEOU). The degree to which a person perceives that making use of a platform would improve productivity is what is meant by the term PU. On the other hand, the degree to which a person feels that making use of the platform will be comparatively effortless is what is meant by the term PEOU. The simplicity of TAP’s description of why some people embrace new technologies has contributed to its widespread adoption. Secondly, TAP’s focus on data processes makes it a viable framework for explaining how IT is used by people of all backgrounds and in all parts of the world, using a broad range of technologies. Finally, there is substantial empirical validation for the aggregate pblackictive performance of TAP, that is supported by a solid conceptual foundation that includes thoroughly investigated and established psychometric indicators (Natasia et al. 2022; Usman et al. 2022).

TAP has been criticised for not being able to take into account enabling conditions as a factor in tech adoption (Ly et al. 2023; Thomas et al. 2023; Malatji et al. 2020), but this doesn’t seem to take away from the model’s success in general. The argument put forth is that community values could be viewed as independent parameters since they are embedded in the results (Lin et al. 2020; Rezaei et al. 2019). Researchers have mostly employed TAP in workplaces where staff members have to utilise a new technological device before they are allowed to opt out of doing so Shin et al. (2019); Ninaus et al. (2021). Furthermore, TAM is primarily conceived as a scheme to clarify personal decisions, although technological choices are frequently made in concert with others (Alshurideh et al. 2023). Hence, TAP’s failure to account for cultural factors is a major flaw. Researchers have proposed that an individual’s behaviour is most accurately characterised by their involvement with community organisations rather than their absence from them Putranto et al. (2023); Tharkude (2023).

Academics have proposed that a person makes decisions as a member of a community unit, and that connections between members of that community can lead to increased consumer participation and devotion (Santos et al. 2022). Furthermore, social media platforms encourage communication and collaboration between members of the group (Abbas et al. 2022). Professional productivity (Zimmer 2022), staff turnover (Boland et al. 2023), creativity (Zimmer 2022), immoral practises (Khan et al. 2023), entrepreneurs (Lacarcel and Huete 2023), and consumer gadget use are only some of the behavioural effects that have been explained by research into the impact of social relationships via social media platforms (Lim and Rasul 2022; Ahmed et al. 2022).

Information communication technologies (ICT) serves as a broad term encompassing a diverse array of technologies that empower users to generate, access, distribute, store, manage, and exchange information in a digital framework. This encompasses computer hardware, software applications, mobile phones, computers, network infrastructure, the internet, telecommunications systems, and related services and applications. In recent times, there has been a growing fascination with the potential of computers and the internet to enhance social communication across various levels. This curiosity has driven research and advancements in the realm of ICT and social digital media platform, leading to the emergence of interactive technologies like Web 2.0, often referblack to as participatory technologies as depicted in Fig. 1 (Hu and Yu 2021).

Throughout this analysis, authors took a close look at the research that has been done on how people in different social circles interact with various categories of consumer gadgets. This paper evaluates the conceptual paradigms used in the existing investigation, as well as the dimensions used to assess online platforms, study circumstances, and survey results, in order to determine shortcomings in the literature and potential for future research. The CICR framework was used in the analysis, which is commonly used in clinical studies with strong scientific foundations. Lockwood et al. (2015) say that a modified version of the CICR paradigm, which is based on the traditional CICR, can help researchers come up with clear study hypotheses. The survey questionnaire guided the study’s investigation, which was developed using CICR:

1. 1.

   Which conceptual models are most frequently invoked in attempts to clarify the pblackictive power of cultural connections with regard to consumer technological adoption?
2. 2.

   Can there be coherence between the conceptualization, design, and implementation of important social connectivity structures?
3. 3.

   What types of investigation settings were used in the publications examined?
4. 4.

   Exist commonly studied areas and new tendencies for future research?

A time frame of 10 years between 2010 and 2022 was chosen because the main goal was to focus on the most recent and most important papers. These papers consider changing consumer behavior and social connectivity experiences influenced by recent factors, such as technological advances. Another reason for making this choice was to focus on the many current papers.

The structure of the article is as follows: In Chapter 2, the authors discussed the expanding area of study on social media platforms as a factor influencing technology adoption. The dispersed strategy in the theoretical underpinnings that have been applied is also emphasized. The third chapter offers an overview of the investigation’s procedure that was employed to classify, pick, evaluate, and summarize research on social media platforms and consumer information technology utilization that was accepted for publication within the stated period of the survey. These steps were performed in order to answer the questions posed in the second part. The findings of the 69 publications that were chosen and analyzed are presented in Chapter 4, along with the conclusions that were drawn from the research inquiries that served as a guide. A review of the results makes up the fifth portion of this paper. This article comes to a close with a conclusion and some recommendations for further study in the last part.

## 2 The influence of social media platforms on consumer technological adoption

Academic pursuit of community connections as a factor in consumer technological adoption has increased. According to Pan (2010), a person’s social media platforms affect their confidence, attitudes, and actions. Research has demonstrated that communication of thoughts and ideas during social relationships influences usage patterns (Sheldon 2002; Bilgihan et al. 2016; Siciliano et al. 2017). Nevertheless, the available research demonstrates that the ideological bases, classifications, related concepts, and indicators of social networking were inconsistent, leading to inconsistent and contradictory outcomes that restrict the generalizability of such observations (Meng et al. 2017).

The idea of a social media platform, which comes up a lot in research on networking sites, has been described in different ways in different studies, showing a lack of coherence. In Zhou et al. (2015); Khan et al. (2021) authors figublack out how likely it was that a cultural object on a social media platform would support a product, activity, or point of view. The hypothesis of socio-cultural networks and the Social Data Processing Design (SDPD) served as the foundation for this investigation. The research evaluated societal impact, architectural equivalency, object homology, and pblackisposing variables in order to anticipate acceptance decisions between agents on a social media platform. The investigation’s results demonstrated that societal impact had limited prognostic validity and that pblackisposing variables (undiscoveblack factors) are crucial in pblackicting acceptance likelihood.

Authors in Filieri et al. (2014), investigated the link between connection design as well as acceptance assessments, and quantified media platforms using emulation, management, lock-in, likeness, relative frequency, and group impacts. To do so, they made use of the notion of social media networks. Using data from open applications and action linkage panel statistics, the research found that an individual user’s willingness to adopt a technique was significantly influenced by either their own activities or those of others in the community with whom they are associated. This was found to be the case regardless of whether the user was involved in the development of the technique or not.

In Okello Candiya Bongomin et al. (2018) authors have examined the mitigating impact of social connections in the association among digital payment usage and access to monetary services in sub-Saharan Africa in research that also utilized social media platform theory. The study examined online communities based on the operational quality of connection linkages as defined by node centralization, network size, resilience, and intertextuality to describe their impact on the amount of information shablack and transmitted within social media platforms. The findings from the research were that the presence of both moderate and strong social media site linkages among electronic payment consumers increased access to monetary services. The methodologies and conclusions of the preceding investigations highlight the lack of key indicators for community networking theory, leading to various indicators and results that make it challenging to apply empirical data.

In the study of how people connect with each other, the idea of “social capital” has also become more popular. Theory of social capital says that faith, traditions, and connections between people are assets Mishra (2020). Authors in Sabatini (2009) used the terms joining capital, spanning capital, and connecting capital to describe how social ties affect how people use new technologies. In Lee and Katz (2015) authors investigate into how Korean immigrants’ use of mobile connectivity changed the online communities they were a part of. The research implemented the concepts of constrained cooperation, social networks, and relationship commitment. Utilizing social value, node density, heterogeneity, and centralization, the social media platform concept was operationally defined. The use of linking capital to measure social wealth demonstrated the ability of social data centers (SDCs) to increase connecting social value. Linking capital and bridging capital, however, were not consideblack in this research. In addition, social capital was employed as a term associated with the social network concept instead of a theoretical model, thus illustrating the current ambiguity in the research on social connections as a significant determinant of consumer tech consumption.

In a study that examined the adoption of innovation by agro-food developers through social media platforms authors used the social value concept to clarify the impact of companionship, connecting, and bringing capital on the dispersion of modern farming among many farming communities (Ramirez et al. 2018). The findings suggest that local social connections exerted a greater effect on the judgment calls, attitudes, and behaviors of their participants. Similarly, in research that utilized the community capital concept to clarify the impact of community capital on destination technology acceptance for touristic promotion researchers quantified the concept utilizing bonding capital as well as connecting capital and stretched it with bandwidth utilization, relationship quality, belief, and social rules (Sung et al. 2015). Several dimensions employed to implement social value in the research imposed a major impact on the degree of technology acceptance within the destination promotion company, the analysis suggested. Authors in Micheels and Nolan (2016) employed social value as a category to evaluate its implications in connection to permeable ability and the acceptance of farming technologies in Canadian provinces. The study measublack social value by promoting social engagement, trustworthiness, common identity, and participation in neighborhood organizations. This highlights the heterogeneity that occurs in the use of social capital as a concept and occasionally as a component of social networking analysis.

Similarly, the concept of social learning was applied in the investigation of community connections’ impact on user technological adoption. The idea asserts that societal connections among individuals on a social media platform promote transformation in cognition outside the scope of the individuals or within broader societal entities (Micheels and Nolan 2016). Individuals’ activities in a community are influenced by their network encounters, according to Garip et al. (2020). In their explanation of the use of digital payments on social networking sites, authors contrasted rural and urban Ugandans (Kiconco et al. 2020). The investigation was based on the theory of social learning and operationally defined through monitoring, imitating, hands-on practice, and explicit technical support services provided by social media network players. The investigation found that social networking features pblackict learning more effectively than personal qualities.

In a different study that used the idea of social learning, authors in Vishnu et al. (2019), investigated how landowners’ social media platforms affect how they learn about important cattle equipment. The presence of a competent personality in the group and homogeneous social communities that encouraged the transfer of innovation and creation were both identified as having an impact on social learning. Using the idea of social learning, authors in Murendo et al. (2018) looked at how social media platforms affected how digital payments were used in Uganda. The theory is operationally defined by combining the strong points of the feeble connections concept and the societal assets theory (Lin 2017; Ahmed et al. 2023) with the close link and weaker tie constructions of the theory. According to the data, social group knowledge aided in the spread of information about digital payments and increased their use. Scholars have a hard time using the early theoretical and conceptual structures to study online platforms, as shown by the fact that they use very different methods to implement concepts and metrics for the theory of social learning and try to expand the idea of social learning with structures from other hypotheses.

Previous research is fractublack and results to misunderstanding because of the absence of uniformity in the conceptualization as well as operationalization of components and the assessment elements and levels, as evidenced by the preceding debate. Consequently, it is necessary to conduct a comprehensive scholarly literature survey of investigations on social connectivity and consumer innovation utilization in order to determine known vulnerabilities and prevalent themes that might set the stage for prospective research on simplifying the emphasis on social connectivity as a crucial component in the research on consumer innovation utilization pblackictors.

## 3 Approach

To better understand the connection among social media platforms and consumer technological adoption, an in-depth research analysis is carried out in this research study. A systematic analysis of the articles is a well-thought-out way to look at the body of empirical studies that have already been done. This is achieved through standardized, repeatable procedures to identify relevant papers, select the most pertinent studies, critically evaluate them, and report the findings (Lin 2017). Meta-analyses are thorough and comprehensive, and they provide information regarding the procedures and strategies employed in a particular study (Fisch and Block 2018). Also, because they answer certain research questions, they make it possible to draw valid conclusions.

### 3.1 Planning

The keywords “social media platforms”, “technological consumption,” and “private individuals” were used during the investigation. Because it has been shown that the terms “technology consumption” and “technology acquisition” are often switched, the phrase “technology integration” was added. Throughout the assessment of authentic identified articles, the study verified that only investigations that examined actual consumer technological consumption were preserved, irrespective of whether the study collection employed technology consumption or technology acquisition.

### 3.2 Investigation in previous publications

The investigation took place in two distinct phases. The first investigation was executed on Google Scholar by utilizing keywords “social media platforms and innovations”, “social media platforms and technology usage between specific consumers”, “social media platforms and innovation strategies”, “online communities and digital adoption between participant clients”, “networking sites and technological advancements utilization”, “web 2.0 and innovative technologies utilization between individual end facebook, twitter and new tech acquisition”, and, finally, “networking sites and engineering utilization between individual clients.” The goal of altering the keywords was to verify that the plan had reached a point of fullness when no more articles could be discoveblack. It was found that Google Scholar is a good place to start because it gathers academic papers from different sources. Having Google Scholar, we were able to identify the database systems with the maximum throughput of relevant academic journals by name, which assisted us in identifying the most highly significant and positive sources for an in-depth investigation. The analysis yielded several outcomes with numerous overlapping components. The findings of the analysis are displayed in Table 1.

### 3.3 Investigate related publications highlighted by Google scholar

The results of the preliminary investigation made it possible to move on to the next stage of the search. It was determined which sources had the greatest amount of academic articles included. The options that were mentioned were JSTOR, Taylor & Francis, Sage, Springer, and Science Direct. Wiley Online was also mentioned. Following the aforementioned keywords, a check was performed across all of the indicated repositories. The below sequence was used to analyze and classify the findings: Using the survey’s title to determine the significance of the survey’s findings.

Descriptions were utilized to even further select the published articles that dealt with the connection among social media platforms and technological adoption from those that completed the phase. The analysis rejected any articles that does not use the individual customer as the basis for evaluation. These comprised research with enterprises as the primary unit of investigation. During the screening procedure, only investigations that examined real technology adoption were preserved.

The blackuction of the group of articles to 69 journal articles that satisfied the research goals is depicted in Table 2. Likewise, Fig. 2 depicts the stream of the comprehensive survey’s choosing procedure. The PRISMA flowchart illustrating the selection process of manuscripts included in a comprehensive literature survey. There are four key phases in this systematic approach. In the Identification phase, an integrated search was conducted using Google Scholar, which resulted in an initial pool of 364,016 articles. After eliminating duplicate and incorrectly tagged articles, 362,659 were removed, leaving 1357 articles for further consideration based on relevant keywords. During the Screening phase, the abstracts or summaries of the identified articles were examined. This step led to the retention of 295 manuscripts, with 1062 articles excluded for not meeting eligibility requirements. In the Eligibility phase, the full texts of the screened manuscripts were thoroughly reviewed, ultimately shortlisting 88 manuscripts, while 16 were excluded for failing to meet the full-text review criteria. Finally, in the Inclusion phase, 72 manuscripts were selected and included in the literature survey for comprehensive analysis.

The next step was to get information from the publications that had already been looked at and passed the description assessment phase. The authors created an outline that included the following sections: (I) the title of the published article, the researcher(s), the date it was published, and the publishing company; (II) the purpose of the study; (III) the study background; (IV) a description of social media networks and research structures; (V) a description of technological utilization and investigation frameworks; (VI) theoretical underpinnings; (VII) the conceptual model used; (VIII) observations; and (IX) research problems identified. The authors then extracted and compiled the information using this framework.

## 4 Survey outcomes

Survey question 1: What popular conceptual paradigms are applied to clarify social media platforms as a determinant of consumer tech adoption?

### 4.1 Disintegration of conceptual paradigms

This was evident from publications that identified social media platforms as a concept underpinned by diverse theories, each with distinct axioms, definitions, and measurable variables. Splitting of theoretical paradigms led to contradictory results and a difficulty extrapolating the results. In literature studies to understand consumer technological adoption, behavioral research and data system concepts, such as data dissemination and the integrated concept of adoption, were used (Ramdhani et al. 2014; Dwivedi et al. 2019; Lai 2017; Venkatesh et al. 2012; Niehaves and Plattfaut 2014; Pai and Huang 2011; Wen et al. 2011; Turel et al. 2011). The various hypotheses are summarized in Table 3 to illustrate the fragmented technique. Survey illustrates the variety of ideas employed to describe social media platforms, as well as the range of theoretical hypotheses established in the research listed in Table 4.

## 5 Survey question 2: Is the operational definition of social media platform components consistent?

The analysis of the academic studies suggests that several theoretical models and categories were employed by previous researchers to substantiate the links that were examined. Sun et al. (2014) utilized social media platform concept and examined the importance of lock-in impact, copying impact, resemblance and authority impacts in a study that investigated the connection among social media sites on the web and technological acceptance. In a research of the interplay among social platforms and protest movements, Jost, Barberá, Bonneau, Langer, Metzger, Nagler, Sterling, Jost et al. (2018), quantified online platforms utilizing sharing of information, inspirational material, and synchronization of activism operations as the research builds, whereas, in an investigation into the connection among networking site connections and talent acquisition, Nayak, Bhatnagar, Bhatnagar and Budhwar (2018), established the Jia (2018), utilized the Bass modelling approach and emphasized on the intensity of connection linkages to implement social media networks employing range value, intimacy, and centralization as the study concepts.

Previous study’s tendency to examine various dimensions and their interrelationships resulted in an upsurge in the segmentation of results, which made it hard to apply them. Intriguingly, there have been limited academic initiatives to incorporate these past research efforts in order to provide an implementation strategy that’d facilitate the generalization of results about the linkages among social media platform and consumer technological consumption variables.

## 6 Survey question 3: What investigation settings did the examined research employ?

According to the examined publications, there is a massive rise in the role played by social connections in affecting customer technology adoption. Frequent studies settings included schooling, entrepreneur, security, employability, farming, and medical. The study of how to utilize technology to enhance social connections through social media platforms has also arisen as a topic of serious importance.

Survey question 4: Are there recurring themes or directions in the studied literature that might inform prospective research?

According to the findings of the survey, three distinct research directions have emerged.

### 6.1 First research direction: the impact of social communication connections on consumer technological consumption

The first direction addressed social connections from a functional standpoint, focusing on how the architecture of societal connections affected consumer technological consumption and mostly relying on social networking modeling theories. Social networking analytics (SNA) is a conceptual paradigm that conceptualizes the architecture of social systems by concentrating on the features of the links linking individuals as opposed to the personal qualities of the members. SNA employs numerical frameworks to determine the functional relationships between endpoints in a social media platform, as well as how their interconnection affects behavior, by utilizing concepts such as extent of primacy, adjacency, connectivity primacy, eigenvalues indispensability, systemic congruence, and connectivity primacy (Ahmed et al. 2022, 2023).

Ludlow and Heydari (2014) used quantitative computational approaches to evaluate the effect of amount of centralization and adjacency within social media platforms in a study on the method for selecting prominent people for promoting a novel item using social media platforms.The research revealed that social connectivity links with the greatest level of centralization and exerts the most influence over item acceptance. Ludlow and Heydari (2014), investigated how social media platforms impacted users’ use of mobile technologies for cooperation. In a regulated field, research involving 327 individuals, networking site analysis to quantify eigenvalues of centralization and connectivity friendliness between all of a social network’s components. Eigenvector centralization evaluates the effectiveness of an unit while taking into account the significance of its neighbors.The results suggest that adding social media platforms to a mobile computing system can make it easier for nodes to share information and learn more.

Hinz et al. (2014) examined the impact of social media platforms on buyer choices in a separate study including 300 respondents. Utilizing amount of centralization (the amount of social relationships a client has inside a connection) between all hubs in the research, analytical graph theory was employed, and it was determined that architectural comparability influenced acceptance of technology.

### 6.2 Second research direction: The impact of social networking connections on consumer technological consumption

The second line of investigation focused on examining the influence of network linkages and actor connections on the utilisation of consumer technology. The concepts of social networks, societal learning, societal capital, and link strength are widely recognised in academic discourse. Partnerships (homophily) were commonly characterised based on several criteria, including the degree of closeness, amount of contact, trustworthiness, and level of likeness. Based on the results of inquiries examining the composition of connections within online social networking platforms, it was observed that the dissemination of perspectives and viewpoints during interpersonal interactions had an impact on patterns of usage Hossain and de Silva (2009).

### 6.3 Third research direction: Social networking platforms and its impact on consumer technological consumption

The third category indicated a growing and dominant investigation into social connections made possible by the proliferation of social media web pages (SMW). The stream also addressed the third survey question regarding developing patterns. Investigating how individuals utilise social media platforms to connect, share information, and affect one another’s decision-making is a phenomenon that is gaining traction in academic studies. The evaluated research revealed an increasing focus in research on the influence technology has had on social media platforms as a result of the rise of technology-driven SMW. The investigations highlighted the degree to which digital has been ingrained in customers’ daily lives and the impact of social media platforms on consumer technological consumption.

This line of research revealed the same heterogeneity of conceptual approaches, categorization of notions, and results as prior studies assessed for this research. Katona et al. (2011); Alvi et al. (2022) utilised the diffusion concept and evaluated extent impact, density of links, and adjacency; whereas they utilised the socialisation concept and evaluated system usage, social involvement, perceptions of the quality, and notoriety; and Peng and Mu (2011) utilised the social media network concept and evaluated lock-in effect, mimicking impact, resemblance impact, leadership impact, and recency effect. ### 13.6 Limitations and unified conceptual framework

This research study offers important insights into the relationship between social media platforms and consumer adoption of digital technologies. However, authors have acknowledged multiple limitations to provide a balanced perspective and guide future research. The selection of articles included in the review may be subject to publication bias, as studies with significant findings are more likely to be published and accessible, potentially overrepresenting certain perspectives. To address this, meta-analytic techniques to quantitatively evaluate the findings of existing research and mitigate biases should be adopted. The reliance on specific keywords and databases might have excluded relevant studies with alternative terminologies or less accessible indexing. Furthermore, the diverse theoretical frameworks and operational definitions in the included studies posed challenges in synthesizing findings, limiting consistent conclusions. Temporal constraints, such as focusing on studies from 2010 to 2022, may have unnoticed earlier foundational research or recent developments, while regional biases in the analyzed studies could restrict generalizability across cultural or socio-economic contexts. This study’s dependence on secondary data from published literature inherently limits the analysis to existing findings, with variations in quality impacting robustness. Lastly, while the CICR framework structublack the analysis effectively, its novel application to this domain may have missed critical dimensions of the interplay between social media and consumer technology adoption.

Future research can focus on developing a unified conceptual framework that integrates the CICR model with key elements from SET and the TAM to address the theoretical fragmentation in studies on consumer technology adoption. By incorporating SET constructs, such as trust and reciprocity, as moderators, and TAM constructs, such as perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness, as mediators, this framework provides a comprehensive approach to understanding the interplay between social media platforms and technology adoption. This unified model not only offers consistency in operational definitions and measurement but also highlights the importance of community dynamics, relational capital, and perceived value in shaping adoption outcomes. Empirical validation of this framework in diverse contexts, including cultural and demographic variations, can further enhance its applicability and relevance, providing actionable insights for both academia and industry.

# PM Modi Unveils 'Sapta Dhara' Vision to Drive India's Next Growth Phase

Prime Minister Narendra Modi, in his Independence Day address, unveiled the 'Sapta Dhara' vision—seven key strengths to drive India's next growth phase toward a 'Viksit Bharat'. He compared it to the historical 'Sapta Sindhu', urging a new current of development. The first stream highlighted is manufacturing power, with a call for end-to-end production and global competitiveness. Modi stressed the next five to seven years as crucial, leveraging youth potential and zero-defect quality.

Aug 15, 2026
· 7 min read

## PM Modi unveils 'Sapta Dhara' vision, says it will drive India's next growth phase

New Delhi, Aug 15

Prime Minister Narendra Modi, in his Independence Day address on Saturday, unveiled the concept of 'Sapta Dhara', describing seven key areas of strength that he said would provide India with the momentum and capabilities required to achieve the next level of growth and build a 'Viksit Bharat'.

Addressing the nation from the ramparts of the Red Fort, PM Modi drew a comparison with the historical idea of 'Sapta Sindhu' (Seven Rivers), saying that India now needs a new current of development and national strength to realise its aspirations for a developed India.

"Today, I would also like to recall that era when the nation... when we knew, understood, and heard of India's prowess in the form of the 'Sapta Sindhu' (Seven Rivers). Now, to build a Viksit Bharat, we need a new current. Today, from the ramparts of the Red Fort, I invoke the 'Sapta Dhara' of strength before the nation," the Prime Minister said.

PM Modi said that the next five to seven years would be particularly important, adding that the combined strength of the seven streams could help India achieve in the coming years what could not be accomplished over several previous decades.

He said the country would also fully harness the power and potential of its youth and integrate their capabilities into the process of nation-building.

"Alongside this, the power and potential of our youth will be fully harnessed and integrated into nation-building. In the coming days, when I speak of Sapta Dhara, the very first stream of power is: Manufacturing Power. My dear fellow citizens, we need to significantly propel our manufacturing sector forward. Along with expanding production, we must manufacture both micro-components and large finished products. The entire value chain must belong to us, and we must carry it forward," he said.

The Prime Minister stressed that India needs to develop not only individual components but also complete products and end-to-end manufacturing capabilities. From designing products to producing them, he said, India should establish itself as a "trusted global supply chain hub".

"To my brothers and sisters working in the manufacturing sector -- this is the right time, this is an opportunity. Do not let this opportunity slip away. To achieve this, we must meet global benchmarks in terms of Cost, Quality, and Scale. Our factories must be competitive, our products user-friendly, and our packaging appealing and attractive to people worldwide. 'Zero Defect' and precision manufacturing must become our defining identity," he said.

PM Modi also emphasised the importance of maintaining international standards in manufacturing and called upon entrepreneurs, manufacturers and MSMEs to use the opportunity to expand India's global footprint.

"When it comes to quality, there should be 'No Compromise'. Therefore, our core mantra must be: 'Quality, Quality, Quality'," he added.

The second stream of the 'Sapta Dhara', according to PM Modi, is Agriculture and Food Production, along with large-scale Food Processing. He said India's farmers now have access to expanding global markets and stressed the need to connect agricultural production with international demand.

"Today, world markets have opened up for our farmers. Because of optics and evolving demand, we are gaining access to a huge market; we need to reach there, and we must seize that space. We need to bridge the journey from farm to export market," the Prime Minister said.

The third stream is Technology and Innovation, which PM Modi described as increasingly important in an era shaped by Artificial Intelligence, Quantum technology, space, robotics and data centres.

"Today is the era of AI, Quantum, Space, Robotics, and Data Centres. An entirely new landscape has unfolded. Emerging technologies are challenging us at every single moment. Therefore, India must not merely remain a consumer market for the world; we must become the Global Hub of Innovation," he said.

PM Modi said India had already demonstrated its technological capabilities through UPI and digital public infrastructure and should now work towards taking its digital public technologies to every part of the world.

The fourth stream of the 'Sapta Dhara' is Gati Shakti, which encompasses infrastructure and connectivity.

"Through Gati Shakti, we must focus on seamless, high-speed connectivity across the country. We need to connect cities via high-speed rail, build modern highways, inland waterways, advanced airports, and robust multimodal logistics systems," he added.

The fifth stream is Raksha Shakti, or Defence Power, which PM Modi said remains critical for India's security and strategic autonomy. He stressed that achieving self-reliance in defence is essential and said India cannot continue to depend on other nations for its defence requirements.

"The importance of defence capability is paramount in every sense. My dear citizens, achieving Aatmanirbharta in defence is essential; India and the world have realised that there is no alternative. When the world looks out for itself, India cannot merely remain an arms market for other nations," he said.

The Prime Minister said India must develop next-generation defence technologies and aim to become a Global Defence Supplier. He highlighted the need to develop capabilities in drone systems, counter-drone systems and hypersonic defence technologies.

He also pointed to cybersecurity as an increasingly important area of defence, saying that the capabilities and talent of India's youth could be used to protect both the country and the wider world.

The sixth stream of the 'Sapta Dhara' is the Green Economy and Blue Economy, which PM Modi said would also create new employment opportunities through green jobs.

"We must achieve global scale in Green Hydrogen, Renewable Energy, Energy Storage, Green Mobility, and Green Manufacturing. While the world continues to deliberate on global warming, India is actively discovering pathways and providing practical solutions to challenges. India is leading with immense capability in the global Green Movement," he said.

PM Modi also highlighted the opportunities available in the Blue Economy because of India's extensive coastline. He said sectors such as fisheries, coastal tourism and ocean technologies could play an important role in India's future economic growth.

The seventh and final stream of the 'Sapta Dhara' is India's Soft Power, which the Prime Minister described as an area of immense importance not only for the country but also for the world.

"India's soft power is truly immense. Today, Yoga has connected the entire world to India. Yoga is becoming a source of energy for humanity and a major pillar of trust in India. For a country rich with centres of faith, Ayurveda, holistic healthcare systems, and the 'Heal in India' initiative, we can showcase our strengths to the world through handicrafts, culture, films, our creative ecosystem, VFX, animation, gaming, and digital content. In the creative world, India can establish its pre-eminence," PM Modi said.

He said India must develop its soft power into a global capability and use its cultural, creative and technological strengths to establish a stronger presence internationally.

"India has provided significant momentum to the WAVES Summit (World Audio Visual & Entertainment Summit), a platform the world eagerly looks forward to, presenting India's soft power and creative talent to the entire world," he added.

Through the 'Sapta Dhara' framework, PM Modi underlined the need for India to simultaneously strengthen manufacturing, agriculture, technology, infrastructure, defence, green and blue economies, and soft power as the country works towards achieving the broader vision of a 'Viksit Bharat'.

— IANS

Residents of Upasnagar and Sindolim staged a protest at Upasnagar Junction on Independence Day, demanding an underpass before the ongoing highway and flyover works are completed.
Locals claim over 3,000 residents are affected by the highway expansion and say the lack of an underpass is creating inconvenience and safety concerns for pedestrians, motorists and residents.

Public Service Transformation: A Literature 
Review on the Role of Technology in Improving 
Service Quality 
 
Soma Gantika*  
 
* Department of Public Administration, Universitas Pasundan, Bandung Jawa Barat, Indonesia.  
Email: laras.puspita12@gmail.com soma.gantika@unpas.ac.id  
 
  
 
ARTICLE HISTORY  ABSTRACT 
 
Received: December 25, 2024 
Revised: January 01, 2025 
Accepted: February 28, 2025 
 
 The application of technology in public services has become an essential topic in 
various discussions on service eﬃciency and quality. However, in Indonesia, the 
implementation of technology in the public sector still faces multiple challenges 
that need to be further analyzed. This research aims to explore the role of 
technology in improving the quality of public services in Indonesia, focusing on e-
government, big data analytics, and artificial intelligence (AI), as well as the 
supporting factors that influence its success. The method used in this research is a 
literature review, which reviews various previous studies on the application of 
technology in the public sector  
in Indonesia and developed countries. 
Technologies such as e-government, big data analytics, and AI have been proven 
to improve the eﬃciency and transparency of public services in developed 
countries. However, in Indonesia, the implementation still faces obstacles, such as 
low digital literacy among employees and the public and resistance to change. 
Factors that support technology implementation include digital literacy, 
organizational readiness, and pro -digitalization government policies. The 
implementation of digital technology has great potential to improve the quality 
of public services in Indonesia. However, existing challenges must be overcome, 
especially regarding infrastructure, digital literacy, and supportive policies. 
Improving digital literacy and organizational readiness are key to successful digital 
transformation in the public sector.
 
 
Keywords: Technology, Public Service, Service Quality. 
 
 
DOI 
https://doi.org/10.52970/grsse.v5i1.952   
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
I. Introduction  
 
Public service is one of the main pillars of realizing good governance. Information technology has 
become a significant catalyst in transforming public services in various countries, including Indonesia, in 
recent decades. The urgency of this research lies  in the increasing public expectations for faster, more 
transparent, and more eﬃcient services. Amid the Industrial Revolution 4.0 phenomenon, the government 
faces significant challenges adapting to digital technology to improve service quality. For example, applying  
technologies such as e- government, artificial intelligence (AI), and big data analytics in the public sector has 
significantly improved  operational eﬃciency and public satisfaction (Dwivedi et al., 2023). However, the 
application of technology in public services in Indonesia still faces various obstacles, such as low digital 
literacy, uneven infrastructure, and resistance to change (Sus anto, 2022). These conditions indicate that

research on the role of technology in improving the quality of public services needs to be carried out 
immediately to answer these challenges. 
One meaningful relationship that is the focus of this research is between technology implementation 
and the quality of public services. Technology enables better accessibility, increased transparency, and 
reduced complex bureaucracy. However, this relation ship is influenced by other variables, such as 
organizational readiness, human resource capability, and government policy support. Previous research, such 
as that conducted by Dwivedi et al. (2023), has shown that implementing digital technology can increa se 
public trust in government. However, these studies focused more on developed countries and less on the 
context of developing countries like Indonesia, which have diﬀerent challenges and dynamics. This creates a 
research gap that needs to be filled through more localized studies (Rahman et al., 2021).  
Other related research, such as that conducted by Susanto (2022), found that low levels of 
implementation still constrain technology adoption in public services in Indonesia due to a lack of integration 
between systems. The study provides an overview but does not yet explain how technology can be optimized 
to improve service quality holistically. In addition, the study by Rahman et al. (2021) highlights the importance 
of digital literacy in successfully implementing technology. However, how this factor aﬀects public service 
satisfaction has not been examined. Thus, there is a research gap in an in-depth analysis of the Indonesian 
context's relationship between technology, service quality, and supporting factors. To conclude, this research 
oﬀers novelty in the form of a comprehensive analysis of the role of technology in improving the quality of 
public services, particularly in Indonesia. This novelty includes an approach emphasizing integrating 
technology with supporting variables, such as digital literacy and human resource capabilities. This research 
is also expected to provide practical benefits for policymakers in formulating eﬀective technology 
implementation strategies. This research aims to identify key factors that influence the successful adoption of 
technology in public services, evaluate its impact on service quality, and provide evidence- based 
recommendations for technology optimization in the context of the Indonesian government. Thus, this 
research not only answers the existing gaps but also makes a real contribution to improving the quality of 
public services in the digital era. 
 
II. Literature Review and Hypothesis Development 
 
2.1. Technology Innovation 
 
Technological innovation refers to creating, developing, and implementing new technology -based 
solutions to improve service eﬃciency and eﬀectiveness. According to Rogers (2003), technological 
innovation in organizations can be adopted through five stages: knowledge, persuasion, decision, 
implementation, and confirmation. In public services, technological innovation includes implementing e -
government systems, using web -based service applications, and integrating data  across agencies (Mergel, 
Edelmann, & Haug, 2019). Ting and Chou (2018) assert that the success of technological innovation depends 
on organizational readiness, policy support, and public acceptance.  In addition, the Technology Acceptance 
Model (TAM) theory developed by Davis (1989) is also relevant in explaining how perceived ease of use and 
technological benefits aﬀect technology adoption in public services.  
 
2.2. Service Quality 
 
Service quality is the extent to which the services can meet or exceed user expectations. According 
to Grönroos (1984), service quality consists of two main dimensions: technical quality (outcome) and 
functional quality (process). Parasuraman, Zeithaml, and Berry (1988), through the SERVQUAL model,  
identified five dimensions of service quality: tangibility, reliability, responsiveness, assurance, and empathy. In 
public services, service quality is often associated with the government's ability to provide fast, accurate,

transparent, and accessible services (Osborne, Radnor, & Nasi, 2013). Liu and Lin (2022) state that technology 
can improve these aspects, but success depends on human resource management and process supervision.  
 
2.3. Community Satisfaction 
 
Community satisfaction refers to the level of conformity between community expectations and the 
reality of the services received. Kotler and Keller (2016) define satisfaction as an emotional response to a 
consumption experience, which reflects an evaluation of whether a service meets or exceeds expectations. In 
the Expectation-Confirmation Model (ECM) theory developed by Oliver (1980), satisfaction is influenced by 
initial expectations, perceived performance, and the level of confirmation of expectations. In the context of 
public services, public satisfaction is often used as an indicator of the success of service transformation, 
focusing on aspects of speed, accessibility, and fairness in service distribution (Brinkerhoﬀ & Brinkerhoﬀ, 2015). 
 
2.4. Implementation of Technology in Public Services 
 
Implementing technology in public services is often influenced by infrastructure readiness, human 
resources, and organizational culture (Li et al., 2022). A study by Mergel et al. (2019) shows that successful 
technology transformation requires a holistic approach involving all stakeholders. This includes strategic 
planning, team member  training, and monitoring of program implementation.  Conversely, technology 
implementation failures are often caused by a lack of integration between technology systems and existing 
business processes (Heeks, 2018). Janssen et al. (2015) added that bureaucratic complexity is also a significant 
obstacle to digital transformation in the public sector. 
 
2.5. Key Factors for Successful Technology Transformation 
 
Based on the literature review, several key factors influence the success of technological 
transformation in public services: 
 
1. Infrastructure Readiness: Adequate technological infrastructure is the main prerequisite for 
supporting digital systems (Zhang, 2020). 
2. Human Resource Competencies: Training and developing  digital competencies for government 
employees is essential to support technology implementation (Liu & Lin, 2022).  
3. Change Management: The government must manage resistance to change through eﬀective 
communication and active participation from all relevant parties (Osborne et al., 2013).  
4. Public Education: Provide digital literacy to the community to ensure maximum accessibility and 
utilization of services (Smith et al., 2023). 
 
III. Research Method 
 
The research method in this literature review will focus on a systematic and comprehensive analysis 
of the existing literature on the role of technology in improving the quality of public services, with particular 
emphasis on the Indonesian context. This research uses a literature review approach that aims to identify and 
analyze various previous studies relevant to this topic. 
 
3.1. Literature Sources 
 
The literature sources used in this research include journal articles, books, research reports, and case 
studies from various international and national publications. The focus  will be on publications related to the 
application of technology in the public sector, especially in developing countries such as Indonesia. Some

topics that will be explored include e-government, big data analytics, artificial intelligence, digital literacy, and 
other supporting factors in public services (Heeks, 2018; Mergel, 2019). 
 
3.2. Literature Selection Criteria 
 
1. Relevance: The literature selected must be directly related to the research topic, namely , technology 
in public services and its impact on service quality (Mergel, 2019).  
2. Quality: Focus on literature published in reputable scientific journals, government research reports, 
and publications from international institutions (Heeks, 2018). 
3. Indonesian context: Paying particular attention to research that addresses the application of 
technology in Indonesia, although global studies are also needed to provide a broader perspective 
(Setiawan & Aryanto, 2020). 
 
3.3. Data Analysis 
 
 The analysis approach used is thematic analysis. Each study reviewed will be analyzed based on key 
themes that emerge in the context of technology, service quality, and other supporting factors such as digital 
literacy and human resource capabilities. Thi s analysis will help identify existing studies' trends, gaps, and 
diﬀerences and relate the findings to Indonesia's challenges (Setiawan & Aryanto, 2020). 
 
3.4. Theory Synthesis and Development 
 
After the analysis, the results of the literature review will be synthesized to build a theoretical 
framework regarding the relationship between technology implementation, service quality, and supporting 
factors in the Indonesian context. This framework is expected to contribute to developing  theories about 
digital transformation in the public sector (Heeks, 2018). 
 
3.5. Practical Implications 
 
This research not only focuses on theory but also provides  practical recommendations for 
policymakers and practitioners in the public sector, especially in formulating technology implementation 
strategies to improve public service quality . These recommendations will be based on the findings of the 
existing literature review, with an emphasis on solutions that fit the local challenges in Indonesia (Mergel, 
2019). 
 
IV. Results and Discussion 
 
The results of this study are based on the analysis of the literature review conducted, with the 
following main findings: 
 
4.1. Application of Technology in Public Services 
 
Technologies such as e- government, big data analytics, and artificial intelligence (AI) have been 
proven to improve the eﬃciency and quality of services in developed countries. These technological 
innovations contribute significantly to creating a more transparent, responsive, and eﬃcient system. However, 
in Indonesia, the application of these technologies still faces various challenges that hinder their optimization. 
One of the main obstacles is the uneven integration of systems in various service sectors, which causes process 
fragmentation and ineﬃciency. In addition, team member  resistance to change is a significant obstacle that 
slows the adoption of new technologies. Nevertheless, technology -based public services still show great

potential to improve transparency and eﬃciency, although realization on the ground is often far from 
expectations (Mergel, 2019; Heeks, 2018). 
 
4.2. Supporting Factors for Technology Implementation 
 
Low digital literacy among government employees and the public is one of the main barriers to 
technology implementation in the public sector. Studies show that high digital literacy is important  in 
accelerating technology adoption, making  it easier for individuals to understand and utilize technology 
eﬀectively (Setiawan & Aryanto, 2020). In addition, organizational readiness is also a crucial factor in successful 
technology implementation. Organizations with a work culture supporting innovation and change tend to be 
more successful in adopting and managing digital transformation. Therefore, policies that encourage such 
changes are indispensable. Governments with  clear policies and support for digital transformation can 
encourage accelerating technology implementation, especially in remote areas often left behind regarding 
digital infrastructure and resources (Mergel, 2019; Choudrie & Dwivedi, 2021).  
 
4.3. Impact of Technology on the Quality of Public Services 
 
Technology has great potential to increase transparency, speed up bureaucratic processes, and 
reduce corrupt practices in public services. Eﬀective technology adoption can facilitate better oversight and 
make it easier for people to access public services  more eﬃciently. However, the successful implementation 
of these technologies largely depends on how well  they can be appropriately  integrated into the existing 
public service system. In addition, the government's readiness to manage the changes that come with digital 
transformation also plays an important role. Without adequate readiness in terms of infrastructure, team 
member training, and policy adjustments, technology's potential to improve public service quality will not be 
fully realized (Setiawan & Aryanto, 2020). 
 
4.4. Discussion  
The application of technology in public services in Indonesia shows excellent  potential to improve 
the quality of services  but still faces various challenges. Technologies like  e-government, big data analytics, 
and artificial intelligence (AI) have proven eﬀective in developed countries, where digital innovation can 
create more transparent, eﬃcient, and responsive service systems (Alshehri & Drew, 2010; Rana et al., 2015). 
Although various technology initiatives have begun to be implemented in Indonesia , such as e -government 
in several regions, technology implementation is often hampered by factors such as resistance to change and 
lack of system integration (Susanto et al., 2021). This shows that although technology has the potential to 
improve public services, its success is highly dependent on readiness and a strategic  approach to its 
implementation.  
Supporting factors such as digital literacy are one of the most influential aspects of the success of 
technology implementation. Previous research has shown that low levels of digital literacy among 
government employees and the public are the main obstacles to eﬀective technology adoption (Setiawan & 
Aryanto, 2020). High digital literacy aﬀects technical skills and increases community participation in 
technology-based services (Choudrie & Dwivedi, 2021). In addition, organizational readiness is also the key to 
success. Organizations with  an adaptive work culture and support digital innovation are more receptive to 
change than resistive organizations (Mergel, 2019). In this context, Heeks' (2018) research highlights the 
importance of the readiness of bureaucratic structures to adopt technology, especially in developing 
countries. 
Government policies are also important in accelerating digital transformation in the public sector. 
Choudrie and Dwivedi (2021) found that governments with consistent policies that support digitalization are 
more successful in integrating technology into service systems. In Indonesia, although there are regulations 
such as the Presidential Regulation on Electronic -Based Government Systems (SPBE), their implementation is

often uneven, especially in remote areas. The study by Dwivedi et al. (2020) emphasized that policies that 
provide strategic direction and technical and funding support are needed to overcome this obstacle.  
The impact of technology on the quality of public services is very significant if appropriately 
managed. Technology can increase transparency, accelerate bureaucratic processes, and reduce corruption, 
as found in studies by Heeks (2018) and Rana et al. (2015). However, this impact can only be achieved if the 
technology system is fully integrated into the public service process. System fragmentation, as reported by 
Susanto et al. (2021) in Indonesia, can hinder eﬃciency and create new challenges. Therefore, strengthening 
system integration and team member  training is crucial. This study provides important implications for 
policymakers and practitioners in the public sector. In the short term, eﬀorts to improve digital literacy among 
employees and the public should be a priority. As suggested by Mergel et al. (2019), continuous training can 
help improve employees' capabilities in managing technology. In addition, investment in digital 
infrastructure, especially in remote areas, must be increased to ensure equitable access to technology. In the 
long term, the government must create policies supporting  digital transformation and  encourage synergy 
between various agencies in building an integrated and sustainable system.  
 
V. Conclusion 
 
Based on the literature review results on the application of technology in public services, it can be 
concluded that technology, such as e- government, big data analytics, and artificial intelligence (AI), has 
excellent potential to improve public service eﬃciency, transparency, and quality. In developed countries, 
technology has successfully optimized the public service process. However, in Indonesia, the application of 
technology still faces various challenges, such as limited infrastructure, team member  resistance to change, 
and low digital literacy among the community and government employees. The main supporting factors for 
the success of technology implementation include higher digital literacy, organizational readiness to adopt 
technology, and government policies that support digital transformation. The central government needs to 
pay special attention to developing policies that encourage the adoption of technology in remote areas and 
increasing digital literacy among employees and the community to accelerate the implementation of 
technology eﬀectively.  The positive impact of technology on public services is highly dependent on 
integrating technology into existing systems and the government's readiness to manage these changes. 
Without adequate readiness, the application of technology may fail to achieve t he desired goals. Therefore, 
the government needs to ensure strong policy support and the provision of adequate infrastructure so that 
digital transformation in public services can occur properly.  Although the challenges are significant, with the 
right approach to increasing digital literacy, policy support, and organizational readiness, technology has 
great potential to improve the quality of public services in Indonesia.

title: The Pillars and Wheel Framework: A Systematic Approach to Studying Technology Ecosystems
content:
# The Pillars and Wheel Framework: A Systematic Approach to Studying Technology Ecosystems

As new technologies emerge, from blockchain to artificial intelligence, countries often rush to adopt them. For any new technology to be successfully implemented in a new country, it’s essential to understand the entire ecosystem in which it will operate, identifying the critical components and the key players involved. A sustainable and well-balanced ecosystem of any technology should rely on solid foundations. It requires a holistic approach, with a well-functioning regulatory framework, digitised processes, informed stakeholders, a well-educated workforce, innovative entrepreneurs, and, ultimately, a clear governance structure.

To address this, we developed the Pillars and Wheel Framework, a comprehensive model that helps to systematically study any technology ecosystem (drones, AI, blockchain, etc.). Initially designed for Nepal’s drone technology ecosystem, this framework is adaptable and can be applied to any emerging technology, such as blockchain, AI and more. The framework is divided into two main categories: the Pillars of a Technology Ecosystem and the Actor Categories of a Technology Ecosystem. These two components help break down the ecosystem into its fundamental parts, which can be systematically studied for a comprehensive understanding.

Pillars of a Technology Ecosystem:

The pillars of a technology ecosystem refer to the core components that ensure its strength and functionality. These pillars need to be robust and interconnected for the ecosystem to thrive.

* Pillar 1 - Regulatory Frameworks and Standards. A regulatory framework includes all the legal and policy structures that guide the development, deployment, and utilization of technology. For example, in the AI sector, this pillar might involve the creation of laws around data privacy, the ethical use of AI, and ensuring transparency in AI algorithms. A solid regulatory framework ensures that the technology operates legally and ethically, helping to protect both consumers and developers.
* Pillar 2 - Capacity Building and Education: This pillar focuses on developing a skilled workforce to support the ecosystem. This pillar encompasses both formal education (such as university degrees and technical certifications) and informal training (such as workshops and online learning opportunities). The ecosystem must have access to an educated, skilled labour force capable of understanding and applying the technology. In the case of AI, this would involve data scientists, machine learning engineers, and researchers. Without capacity building, the ecosystem will lack the necessary talent to innovate and maintain technological advancements.
* Pillar 3 - Business Support and Innovation: This pillar deals with the infrastructure and resources needed to support businesses as they develop and scale new technologies. This includes access to financial capital, incubators, accelerators, and networking opportunities that allow startups and businesses to thrive. Business support helps foster an environment of innovation, where companies are encouraged to take risks and invest in new ideas. In the case of AI, it could include venture capital funding for AI startups or collaborative efforts between tech companies and research institutions to bring new products to market.
* Pillar 4 - Community Engagement and Awareness. This pillar is crucial for ensuring that the technology is integrated into the broader society. Community engagement refers to raising awareness and educating various stakeholders, including the public, civil society organizations, and industry groups, about the technology and its potential impact. In AI, this could involve outreach programs to inform people about the benefits and risks of AI, as well as initiatives to ensure the technology is inclusive and accessible. Engaging with the community fosters broader acceptance of the technology and helps drive its successful integration into society.

Actor Categories of a Technology Ecosystem:

## Recommended by LinkedIn

While the pillars define what enables a technology ecosystem to function, the actors define who drives it forward. The actors are the key players who drive the ecosystem forward. These include individuals, organizations, and groups that play various roles in developing, deploying, and influencing the ecosystem.

* Academic Stakeholders: This includes academic institutions and training providers. These entities are responsible for educating the next generation of professionals and researchers, as well as conducting research and development that drives innovation. Universities and training providers in the AI ecosystem, for instance, provide essential education and training in fields like machine learning, data science, and computer vision, contributing to the growth of the ecosystem.
* Government Stakeholders: Government entities play a critical role in shaping the regulatory environment, creating policies, and enforcing laws that guide the development of the ecosystem. There are two sub-categories within this group. The first sub-category, Regulatory Actors, involves agencies responsible for creating and enforcing regulations that ensure technology is used ethically and safely. For example, governments may enact laws on data protection, intellectual property, and the ethical use of AI. The second sub-category, Tech Application actors, refers to government entities that use technology directly in the public sector. These agencies drive demand for technology by adopting solutions that improve public services such as healthcare, transportation, and security. Governments can stimulate innovation by being early adopters of AI technologies and integrating them into public sector services.
* Non-Government Stakeholders: This includes development partners, non-profit organizations, private sector actors, and freelancers. These stakeholders often work outside of the governmental framework, but they play an essential role in the ecosystem. Development partners and non-profits can provide funding, resources, or knowledge transfer to support the development of technology in emerging markets. Private sector companies are typically responsible for developing and commercializing technology products and services. Freelancers and individual innovators also play a significant role by contributing their expertise and creativity to projects within the ecosystem.

### Expanding the Framework for AI and Other Technologies: A Call to Action

The Pillars and Wheel Framework was initially developed through our study of Nepal’s drone ecosystem (you can access the summary document about the study here). However, we strongly believe that its potential extends far beyond drones and can be adapted to study any emerging technology. Every country’s ecosystem is unique, and this framework can be customized to address local challenges and seize new opportunities, making it versatile and applicable globally.

This is where we need your collaboration.

If you’re interested in exploring how this framework can be applied to your country for a specific technology initiative, we would love to collaborate with you. We also invite you to help identify organizations in other countries focused on supporting the growth and scaling of frontier technologies. Together, we can leverage, contextualize and update this framework to build a deep understanding of each ecosystem and craft smarter, more effective strategies for sustainable growth and innovation.

Let’s work together to expand this framework to help institutionalize emerging technologies, strengthen governance systems, and foster sustainable, inclusive growth across global technology sectors.

For collaboration opportunities, please reach out to us at uttam@naxa.com.np and business@naxa.com.np.
